title: Some Great Lakes Fish May Be Older Than Your Whole Family Tree
summary: Imagine a fish that was already swimming around when the first telescope spotted Jupiter's moons. That's about 400 years ago. A new study says some lake sturgeon in the Great Lakes might be that old — or even older. Lake sturgeon are huge, armored-looking fish, four to six feet long and up to 80 pounds. Their ancestors swam with dinosaurs 200 million years ago. Scientists used to think they lived 50 to 100 years. The oldest one ever caught was 154 years old, back in 1953. But counting a fish's age is tricky. Fish have dark rings on their scales or fin spines — one ring per year. The problem? In very old, slow-growing sturgeon, the rings get squished together and you can't tell them apart. So researchers tried something different. From 1980 to 2024, they caught thousands of sturgeon in five Great Lakes waterways, measured them, and put tiny ID tags under their skin — like the microchips vets put in cats and dogs. When they caught the same fish again years later, they could see how much it had grown. From that, they calculated ages. Some males might reach 435 years. "All sturgeon species now need to be reassessed," says one scientist who wasn't part of the study. Others say we need more tests to be sure.
why_it_matters: Animals that live for centuries grow slowly and have few babies, so learning their real age helps people protect them before they disappear.

background_read: The Great Lakes (five huge lakes along the border of the United States and Canada — Superior, Michigan, Huron, Erie, and Ontario) hold about one-fifth of the world's fresh surface water.
Lake sturgeon are ancient fish: their family line is far older than most dinosaurs, and they were once so common that people caught them by the thousands.
Scientists often estimate a fish's age by counting rings on its scales or fin spines, the same way tree rings show how old a tree is.
Article_Structure: WHO: Scientists who caught, measured, and tagged thousands of lake sturgeon, plus an outside scientist who commented on the study
WHAT: A new study suggests some lake sturgeon may live far longer than people thought — possibly more than 400 years
WHERE: Five waterways in the Great Lakes, with tagging work done from 1980 to 2024
WHY: If the ages are right, scientists must rethink how long fish can live and how to protect them

perspectives.description: If sturgeon can live for centuries, we may have been badly underestimating many other long-lived animals too.
The new tag-and-measure method still needs more tests before everyone accepts ages of 400 years or more.
A fish that takes a very long time to grow up is easy to wipe out, so protection rules may need to change to match its slow life.
